Cada satélite del GPS envía sin parar un: Each GPS satellite continuously sends a message with the exact time at which it transmits it. Your phone receives it a moment later and, since the signal travels at the speed of light, $c = 299,792,458 "m/s"$, it calculates how far away the satellite is: $d = c · Δt$.\n\nWith the distance to four satellites (three for the position and one more to adjust the phone's clock) it knows where you are within a few metres. Everything depends on the satellites' clocks being perfectly synchronised: an error of $1 "µs"$ is $c · 1 "µs" ≈ 300 "m"$.
is the speed of a GPS satellite at 20,200 km height: one orbit every 11 h 58 min.
Cada satélite lleva relojes atómicos, ta: Each satellite carries atomic clocks, so accurate that they do not drift by a second in hundreds of thousands of years. Before launch they are set to the time of the ones on Earth.\n\nBut the satellites are not at rest: they orbit at $r = 26,560 "km"$ from the centre of the Earth with $v = √(G M/r) = 3874 "m/s"$, and they are much further from the mass of the Earth than we are. Relativity says that both things change the rate of a clock, each in a different direction.

La relatividad especial dice que un relo: Special relativity says that a moving clock runs slower seen from Earth. With speeds small compared with light, each second loses $v^2/(2c^2) = 8.3·10^{-11} "s"$.\n\nIn one day, $86,400 "s"$, that is $7.2 "µs"$ of lag. It seems little, but for an atomic clock it is enormous. Move the slider to see how it grows with speed.

La relatividad general dice que un reloj: General relativity says that a clock runs faster the less gravity it feels. At a height of 20,200 km the gravitational potential is less negative than on the ground, and the clock gains $Δφ/c^2 = G M (1/R_T − 1/r)/c^2$ per second, with $R_T = 6371 "km"$.\n\nIt comes to $5.29·10^{-10}$ per second: $45.7 "µs"$ per day, more than six times what it loses because of speed. Change the height of the orbit and see when each effect wins.
